messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Chloe, a 28-year-old police officer, sat rigidly in the chair, her hands clasped so tightly her knuckles were white. For six months, since what she only referred to as "the incident," she had felt a fundamental shift inside her, as if a switch had been flipped, plunging her world into a constant, humming state of high alert. It was a state she could no longer endure, and it had finally brought her to therapy.

The incident had occurred on a routine domestic call-out. She and her partner of three years, an officer she had trusted implicitly, had entered a tense but verbally contained argument between a couple. Chloe had been de-escalating, her training kicking in, when her partner suddenly moved past her. Without warning, he struck the man, who was already raising his hands in compliance. The assault was brutal and swift. What stayed with Chloe was not just the sight but the full sensory imprint: the sickening, wet crack of bone, the coppery smell of blood that seemed to fill the air instantly, and the feeling of her own body locked in place, utterly frozen.

In the aftermath, an internal review cleared her partner, a decision that shattered Chloe’s faith in the very system she had sworn to uphold. This institutional validation of the violence cemented a profound sense of betrayal that began to colour her entire worldview. She had come to believe that the world was not a place of order she helped maintain, but a fundamentally dangerous and unpredictable arena where violence could erupt from anyone, at any time. This conviction that she had been betrayed by someone she trusted meant she now saw potential threats everywhere, especially within her own precinct.

This pervasive sense of danger now primes her for the past to constantly intrude upon the present. At work, she finds herself watching her new partner’s hands, scrutinizing his posture for the slightest sign of tension, a constant monitoring that exhausts her. The belief that the world is a dangerous place makes every sudden movement on the street feel like a precursor to violence. This hypervigilance is a trigger in itself; a car door slamming shut or the sharp, metallic click of a seatbelt can be enough to pull her back into that room. The memory forces its way into her mind, an uncontrolled access she is powerless to stop.

When the memory arrives, it is a complete sensory hijacking. She is no longer in her patrol car or her kitchen but is standing again on that worn linoleum floor, the smell of stale beer and blood in her nostrils, the screams echoing in her ears as if it were all happening for the first time. It feels utterly real. Yet, in these moments, a terrifying disconnect occurs; she feels as if she is watching a movie starring a different person, some other, pathetic officer who just stood there and did nothing. This sense that the memory feels alien, that it belongs to someone else, is perhaps the most disorienting part of the experience.

Each time the memory recedes, it leaves behind a residue of reinforced convictions. The vivid reliving of her own frozen limbs confirms her belief that her body is an enemy, a traitor that will fail her when it matters most. The sheer brutality of the remembered violence reinforces her certainty that the world is an irredeemably dangerous place. And seeing her former partner's face, contorted in a rage she had never imagined, solidifies the raw, painful knowledge of his betrayal, making it feel impossible to ever truly trust a colleague again. This cycle, where her beliefs trigger the memory and the memory hardens her beliefs, has been tightening its grip for months.

The consequences have been devastating for her career. She can no longer perform her duties with the confidence she once had, viewing every interaction through a lens of imminent threat. After a near-fatal hesitation during a traffic stop last month, she has been on extended leave, unable to bring herself to put on the uniform. She finally sought help because she is terrified of losing the job that once defined her, but even more so, she is afraid of losing herself completely to the image of that frozen, helpless officer she sees in her mind.
